note: Subjects/Maths/M1 Mechanics 1/3 Kinematics of a particle moving in a straight line.md
outline: Choose a positive direction and use signed displacement $s$, initial velocity $u$, final velocity $v$, constant acceleration $a$ and time $t$. The constant-acceleration equations include $v=u+at$, $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$, $s=\tfrac12(u+v)t$ and $v^2=u^2+2as$. Select an equation containing the known quantities and the unknown, then check the sign and units. The gradient of a displacement–time graph is velocity; the gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration. Signed area under velocity–time gives displacement, while area under speed–time gives distance. Area under acceleration–time gives change in velocity. A straight velocity–time line represents constant acceleration; the corresponding displacement–time curve is quadratic.

misconceptions.statement: Initial velocity can be ignored when finding final velocity or displacement.
misconceptions.refutation: Initial velocity contributes $u$ to $v=u+at$ and $ut$ to $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$.
misconceptions.contrast: Even before acceleration acts, the particle may already be moving.

misconceptions.statement: Area below the time axis on a velocity–time graph counts positively towards displacement.
misconceptions.refutation: Velocity is signed, so area below the axis is negative displacement.
misconceptions.contrast: For distance, add the magnitudes of all areas.

misconceptions.statement: The gradient of a velocity–time graph gives displacement.
misconceptions.refutation: The gradient is change in velocity divided by time, which is acceleration.

misconceptions.statement: The acceleration contribution to displacement is $at^2$.
misconceptions.refutation: For constant acceleration it is $\tfrac12at^2$ because velocity rises linearly.
misconceptions.contrast: The acceleration contribution is the triangular area under a velocity–time line.

misconceptions.statement: A negative acceleration always means a particle is slowing down.
misconceptions.refutation: Negative acceleration means acceleration points in the negative chosen direction.
misconceptions.contrast: If velocity is also negative, speed increases.

misconceptions.statement: The signed area under an acceleration–time graph gives the velocity itself.
misconceptions.refutation: Accumulating acceleration over time gives the change in velocity, so the area must be added to the initial velocity to obtain the velocity at the end of the interval.
misconceptions.contrast: With $u=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and a total signed area of $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the final velocity is $7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, not $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

misconceptions.statement: Always discard one of two positive time roots.
misconceptions.refutation: Check both against the interval: a particle can pass the same height twice. Only reject a root for a physical or stated-domain reason.
misconceptions.contrast: A numerical question appears to require one answer.
misconceptions.source: SaveMyExams XMA01 c2.2.pdf pp.2–4; P1-1.5 algebraic time-domain reasoning

misconceptions.statement: One average acceleration works in every suvat equation across several stages.
misconceptions.refutation: Apply suvat separately in each constant-acceleration interval, carrying velocity and position continuously across the boundary.
misconceptions.contrast: A single formula feels shorter than treating each interval.
misconceptions.source: SaveMyExams XMA01 c2.1.pdf pp.14–17; XMA01 c2.2.pdf p.2

worked.problem: A particle has initial velocity $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and constant acceleration $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $4\,\mathrm{s}$. Find its final velocity and displacement.

steps.do: Choose the direction of motion as positive and list $u=3$, $a=2$, $t=4$.
steps.why: Signed values must be consistent before selecting equations.
Acceleration is constant, and this equation uses the three known values.
This equation calculates signed displacement over the whole interval.

faded.problem: A particle has initial velocity $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and constant acceleration $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $4\,\mathrm{s}$. Find its displacement.

items.stem: A particle has initial velocity $[[u]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and constant acceleration $[[a]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Find its velocity after $[[t]]\,\mathrm{s}$.
items.explanation: For constant acceleration, $v=u+at$: add the change in velocity $at$ to the initial velocity.
hints: List the known suvat quantities.
Choose the equation relating initial and final velocity, acceleration and time.
Multiply acceleration by elapsed time before adding initial velocity.

items.stem: A particle moves in a straight line with initial velocity $[[u]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and constant acceleration $[[a]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $[[t]]\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate its displacement.
items.explanation: Use $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$ and include both the initial-velocity and acceleration terms.
hints: Displacement depends on starting velocity as well as acceleration.
Choose the suvat equation without final velocity.
Calculate $ut$ and $\tfrac12at^2$ separately, then add.

items.stem: A particle has initial velocity $[[u]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and constant acceleration $[[a]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Find its displacement when its velocity first reaches $[[v]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
hints: Time is not given.
Use the suvat equation without time.
Subtract the squared initial velocity from the squared final velocity.

items.stem: A particle starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $[[a]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $[[t1]]\,\mathrm{s}$, then travels at its attained constant speed for $[[t2]]\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the total distance.
items.explanation: The velocity–time graph has a triangle during acceleration and a rectangle at constant speed; their areas add to the distance.
hints: Split the journey into two intervals.
Find the final speed of the accelerating interval.
Add the triangle area to the rectangle area beneath the velocity–time graph.

items.stem: A particle moves at $[[u]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the positive direction and has constant acceleration $-[[b]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $[[t]]\,\mathrm{s}$. Find its total distance travelled.
items.explanation: The particle turns at $u/b$ seconds. Add the positive outward distance $u^2/(2b)$ and the distance after reversal $\tfrac12b(t-u/b)^2$.
hints: Check whether velocity changes sign.
Find the turning time using $v=u-bt$.
Find the two positive distances on either side of the turn and add.

items.stem: State what the gradient of a velocity–time graph represents.
items.explanation: The gradient is change in velocity divided by change in time: acceleration. Displacement comes from signed area under the graph.
hints: Think of rise divided by run.
The vertical axis measures velocity and the horizontal axis measures time.
Write the units of the gradient.

items.stem: A velocity–time graph has a straight line from $0$ to $4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ over $2\,\mathrm{s}$, then a straight line to $-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ over the next $3\,\mathrm{s}$. State the displacement over the $5\,\mathrm{s}$.
items.explanation: The first triangle has area $4$ m. The second trapezium has signed area $3$ m, giving $7$ m; adding the area below the axis positively gives distance, not displacement.
hints: Areas below the time axis have a negative sign.
Split the graph into the first triangle and the later trapezium.
Use average velocity times time for each straight segment.

items.stem: Explain how displacement, velocity, speed and acceleration can be read from displacement–time, velocity–time, speed–time and acceleration–time graphs.
items.explanation: A graph gradient compares change in the vertical quantity with time; an area multiplies the vertical quantity by time. Keep the sign for vector quantities.
hints: Match the vertical axis to the quantity.
Use slope for rates of change and area for accumulated change.
Distinguish signed velocity from nonnegative speed.

rubric.point: The gradient of a displacement–time graph gives velocity.
The gradient of a velocity–time graph gives acceleration.
Signed area under velocity–time gives displacement, while area under speed–time gives distance.
Signed area under acceleration–time gives change in velocity.

items.stem: A particle has velocity $-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and constant acceleration $-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Explain what happens to its speed over the next second and why.
items.explanation: Using $v=u+at$ gives $v=-5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ after one second. The speed is its magnitude, $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so negative acceleration does not by itself mean slowing.
hints: Keep direction signs separate from speed.
Use $v=u+at$ for one second.
Compare the magnitudes of the initial and final velocities.

rubric.point: Its speed increases from $3$ to $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Velocity and acceleration point in the same negative direction, so the magnitude of velocity increases.

items.stem: Sketch a velocity–time and a displacement–time graph for a particle starting with positive velocity and moving with constant negative acceleration, until it stops. Label each graph’s key features.
items.explanation: Constant negative acceleration gives a linearly decreasing velocity. Because displacement gradient equals velocity, the displacement curve rises but flattens to a horizontal tangent at rest.
hints: A constant acceleration fixes the velocity graph gradient.
Velocity is the displacement graph gradient.
Mark the stop where velocity reaches zero.

rubric.point: Velocity–time is a straight line with negative gradient from positive velocity to zero.
Displacement–time rises with decreasing gradient and reaches a horizontal tangent at the stop.

items.stem:
A particle starts from rest at $t=0$ and moves in a straight line. Its acceleration is $4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $0\le t<3$, zero for $3\le t<5$, and $-6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $5\le t\le 8$, where $t$ is measured in seconds.
(a) Sketch the speed–time graph for $0\le t\le 8$, labelling the speed at $t=3$, $t=5$ and $t=8$ and the time at which the particle is momentarily at rest.
(b) Hence find the total distance travelled during the $8\,\mathrm{s}$.

scheme.point: (a) Builds the velocity interval by interval from rest, using the signed area of the acceleration–time graph or $v=u+at$ on each interval: $v=12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $t=3$ and still $12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $t=5$.
(a) Uses $v=12-6(t-5)$ on the last interval, so $v=0$ at $t=7\,\mathrm{s}$ and $v=-6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $t=8$.
(a) Sketch shows a straight line from the origin to $(3,12)$, a horizontal segment to $(5,12)$ and a straight line falling to $(7,0)$.

(a) Sketch shows the final second as speed rising from $0$ at $t=7$ to $6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $t=8$, that is the negative velocity drawn as a positive speed, with $t=7$ labelled as the instant of rest.
(b) Adds the areas of all four parts of the speed–time graph: $\tfrac12(3)(12)+2(12)+\tfrac12(2)(12)+\tfrac12(1)(6)$.

items.explanation: Each interval of constant acceleration adds its signed area to the velocity, giving $0\to12$, then $12$, then $12\to-6$. Speed is the magnitude, so the speed–time graph touches zero at $t=7\,\mathrm{s}$ and rises again; its total area is the distance, $57\,\mathrm{m}$, whereas the displacement is only $51\,\mathrm{m}$.
hints: The acceleration graph tells you how the velocity changes, not what it is, so you also need the starting value.
Work along the motion one interval at a time, carrying the end velocity of each interval into the next, then take magnitudes to get speed.
On $5\le t\le 8$ write $v=12-6(t-5)$ and solve $v=0$ to find where the graph meets the time axis.

items.stem: A particle moving in a straight line has velocity $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $t=0$. Its acceleration–time graph is horizontal at $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $0\le t<4$ and horizontal at $-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $4\le t\le 9$, with $t$ in seconds. Find its velocity at $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$.
items.explanation: The signed areas are $3\times4=12$ and $-2\times5=-10$, a total change in velocity of $+2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $v=5+2=7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Quoting $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ treats the area as the velocity itself rather than the change in it, and $27\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ adds the area below the time axis positively.
hints: An area under an acceleration–time graph has the units of a velocity, but it measures a change.
Find the area of each rectangle with its own sign, then combine both with the initial velocity.
The second rectangle lies below the time axis, so its area is $-2\times5$.

items.stem: A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration $a$. Its velocity is $u$ at time $0$ and $v$ at time $t$, and its displacement over that time is $s$. By considering the area under its velocity–time graph, show that $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$.

scheme.point: States that constant acceleration makes the velocity–time graph a straight line from $(0,u)$ to $(t,v)$ whose gradient is $a$, so $v-u=at$.
States that the displacement is the area under that line, and splits it into a rectangle of width $t$ and height $u$ together with a triangle of base $t$ and height $v-u$.

items.explanation: Displacement is the signed area under a velocity–time graph. For constant acceleration that area is a rectangle of area $ut$ plus a triangle of area $\tfrac12t(v-u)$, and the gradient of the line gives $v-u=at$, which turns the triangle into $\tfrac12at^2$.
hints: The command word Show that means every line of the argument must appear, ending at the printed result.
Displacement is the area under the velocity–time graph, and the gradient of that graph is the acceleration.
Draw the straight line from $(0,u)$ to $(t,v)$ and cut the region beneath it into a rectangle and a triangle.

M1-3.1.motivate: A velocity can change even on a straight road, and the signs tell you which way the particle moves. A sketch or a few measured quantities can reveal displacement, distance and acceleration without following every instant of the journey.

discover.stem: On a velocity–time graph, what does the signed area between the graph and the time axis give?
discover.explanation: Velocity multiplied by time gives signed displacement. Area below the axis subtracts from the total; adding its magnitude instead would contribute to distance.

M1-3.1.establish:
Choose a positive direction, then let $s$ be signed displacement, $u$ and $v$ initial and final velocities, $a$ constant acceleration, and $t$ elapsed time. For straight-line motion at constant acceleration, use $v=u+at$, $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$, $s=\tfrac12(u+v)t$, or $v^2=u^2+2as$. Select the equation containing the known values and the quantity sought. On a displacement–time graph, gradient gives velocity. On a velocity–time graph, gradient gives acceleration and signed area gives displacement. On a speed–time graph, area gives total distance. On an acceleration–time graph, signed area gives change in velocity. A horizontal acceleration–time line corresponds to a straight velocity–time line and a quadratic displacement–time curve. Use $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ where gravity is involved, with a sign set by your chosen positive direction.
A fifth form, $s=vt-\tfrac12at^2$, follows from $s=\tfrac12(u+v)t$ with $u=v-at$; none of the five is printed in the paper.
M1-3.1.connect: These equations and graphs describe the same motion: a constant velocity–time gradient is the acceleration, and the area under that line produces $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$. If the line crosses the time axis, split the journey there to calculate distance.
M1-3.1.note:
- Choose one positive direction and keep displacement, velocity and acceleration signed.
- Use a suvat equation only within an interval of constant acceleration.
- Displacement–time gradient is velocity; velocity–time gradient is acceleration.
- Velocity–time signed area is displacement; speed–time area is distance.
- Acceleration–time signed area is change in velocity.
- Learn all five equations, including $s=vt-\tfrac12at^2$: the paper does not give them.
M1-3.1.self_explain: Why does a velocity–time graph crossing below the time axis require two different area calculations for displacement and distance?
M1-3.1.plain_words: Constant acceleration means the velocity changes by the same amount every second, so the velocity–time graph is a straight line. Pick a positive direction, write down the three suvat values you know, and choose the equation that contains them and the one you want. Graphs say the same thing: gradient and area turn one quantity into the next.

prerequisite_bridges.bridge: Choose one positive direction, just as for vector components. A negative velocity means movement in the opposite direction; speed is its magnitude.

Rearrange a time equation to a quadratic, solve both roots, then test each against the specified time interval. A negative root is excluded when time is measured from the stated start; two positive roots may both describe valid visits.

forms.name: Select and apply suvat with signed quantities
wordings: Find the acceleration and elapsed time
Calculate displacement with a chosen positive direction
forms.example:
A particle moves left, changing velocity uniformly from $-2$ to $-8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ over displacement $-15\,\mathrm{m}$. Find acceleration and time.
1. Take right as positive: $u=-2$, $v=-8$, $s=-15$. No time is given, so select $v^2=u^2+2as$.
2. $64=4-30a$, hence $a=-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
3. $v=u+at$ gives $-8=-2-2t$, hence $t=3\,\mathrm{s}$.
4. Check: average velocity is $-5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; multiplying by $3\,\mathrm{s}$ gives $-15\,\mathrm{m}$. Both velocity and acceleration point left, so speed increases.
forms.check: A particle moves right with constant acceleration, changing velocity from $3$ to $9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ through $24\,\mathrm{m}$. Find $a$ and $t$. Explain how its velocity changes in each second.
forms.answer: $a=(9^2-3^2)/(2(24))=1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $t=(9-3)/1.5=4\,\mathrm{s}$. Its velocity increases by $1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ each second.
forms.source: Library: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c2.2.pdf, pp.2–4; bundle M1-3.1.

rubric.point: Uses a valid constant-acceleration relation with the given values, or an equivalent average-velocity method.
Finds acceleration $1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
Finds elapsed time $4\,\mathrm{s}$.
Explains velocity increases by $1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ each second.

retry.check: A particle changes uniformly from $-5$ to $-11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ through $-48\,\mathrm{m}$. Find acceleration and elapsed time.

rubric.point: Uses signed data in a valid constant-acceleration relation; accept average velocity followed by acceleration, including -48=(-5-11)t/2 giving t=6 and a=(-11+5)/6=-1. Credit algebraically equivalent signed substitutions without requiring named formulae or exact wording.
Acceleration $-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
Time $6\,\mathrm{s}$.

forms.name: Solve a time quadratic and select physical roots
wordings: Find the time when the particle reaches the ground
Explain which quadratic roots are physically possible
forms.example:
A particle starts with velocity $-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and constant acceleration $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Find when it first reaches displacement $15\,\mathrm{m}$ after the start.
1. Choose $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$: $15=-2t+t^2$.
2. Rearrange and factor: $t^2-2t-15=(t-5)(t+3)=0$.
3. The roots are $5$ and $-3\,\mathrm{s}$. The specified interval is $t\geq0$, so only $t=5\,\mathrm{s}$ applies.
4. Substitute: $-2(5)+5^2=15$. Never discard a root just because it is smaller: judge against the actual time interval.
forms.check: A stone is projected vertically upward at $4.9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ from $9.8\,\mathrm{m}$ above the ground. Neglect air resistance and use $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Find its time to reach the ground and its impact velocity, taking upward as positive.
forms.answer: $s=-9.8$, $u=4.9$, $a=-9.8$. Thus $-9.8=4.9t-4.9t^2$, so $(t-2)(t+1)=0$. The root $-1\,\mathrm{s}$ precedes projection; impact is at $2.0\,\mathrm{s}$. Then $v=4.9-9.8(2)=-14.7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, or $-15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to 2 s.f.; direction is downward.
forms.source: Library: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c2.2.pdf, pp.2–4; bundle M1-3.1. The quadratic-root selection is algebraic application of P1-1.5, not an audited M1 mark-scheme form.

rubric.point: Assigns downward displacement and acceleration negative.

Uses a valid constant-acceleration method with signed data to determine the impact time and velocity; accept a time quadratic or first finding the downward impact velocity from v^2=u^2+2as and then using v=u+at. Finding both time roots is not required.
Obtains the physically valid time after projection, t=2 s; an explicit explanation of a negative root is not required.
Obtains downward impact velocity -14.7 m s^-1 (or -15 m s^-1 to 2 significant figures).

retry.check: A particle starts with velocity $u=-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and moves with constant acceleration $a=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Find the time after the start when $s=28\,\mathrm{m}$, and explain the rejected root.
retry.answer: $28=-3t+t^2$, so $(t-7)(t+4)=0$. Choose $t=7\,\mathrm{s}$; $t=-4\,\mathrm{s}$ is before the stated start.

rubric.point: Forms a valid quadratic.
Obtains roots $7$ and $-4$.
Identifies rejected root $-4$ as before the start.
Explains the time restriction.

forms.name: Interpret and sketch four motion graphs with reversal and stages
wordings: Sketch displacement–time, velocity–time, speed–time and acceleration–time graphs
Find displacement and distance from a piecewise graph
forms.example:
Start at $s=0$ with $u=6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For $0\leq t\leq4\,\mathrm{s}$ let $a=-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; then keep the resulting velocity for $2\,\mathrm{s}$. Sketch all four graphs and find final displacement and distance.
1. Velocity: $v=6-3t$ until $t=4$, then $v=-6$ to $t=6$. Label $(0,6),(2,0),(4,-6),(6,-6)$ with SI axes. The zero crossing is a reversal.
2. Displacement: $s=6t-1.5t^2$ until $t=4$; it rises from zero to a maximum $6\,\mathrm{m}$ at $t=2$, returns to zero at $t=4$, then follows $s=-6(t-4)$ to $-12\,\mathrm{m}$. The first curve is concave down, with horizontal tangent at reversal; displacement and velocity remain continuous at the stage boundary.
3. Speed: reflect the negative velocity segment upward, giving a V through $(0,6),(2,0),(4,6)$, then a horizontal line to $(6,6)$.
4. Acceleration: horizontal at $-3$ until $t=4$, then at zero. Show a jump at $t=4$, with no sloping connector; the instantaneous boundary value is not specified.
5. Signed velocity areas give $6-6-12=-12\,\mathrm{m}$ displacement. Magnitudes give $6+6+12=24\,\mathrm{m}$ distance.
forms.check: Start at $s=0$, $u=8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Acceleration is $-4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for the first $3\,\mathrm{s}$, then zero until $t=5\,\mathrm{s}$. Sketch and label all four motion graphs. Find total displacement and distance.
forms.answer: Velocity is a straight line through $(0,8),(2,0),(3,-4)$, then horizontal to $(5,-4)$. Displacement is $s=8t-2t^2$ for the first stage: concave down through $(0,0),(2,8),(3,6)$, with horizontal tangent at its maximum. Then $s=6-4(t-3)$, ending at $(5,-2)$, joined continuously with matching slope. Speed is a V through $(0,8),(2,0),(3,4)$ then horizontal to $(5,4)$. Acceleration is $-4$ for the first stage and zero for the second, with a jump at $t=3$. Label time in seconds and the other axes in metres, metres per second and metres per second squared respectively. Areas give displacement $8-2-8=-2\,\mathrm{m}$ and distance $8+2+8=18\,\mathrm{m}$.
forms.source: Library: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c2.1.pdf, pp.14–17; bundle M1-3.1.

rubric.point: Velocity sketch labels the line, reversal and constant second stage.
Reversal occurs at 2 seconds and subsequent velocity is negative.
Displacement sketch has a concave-down curve, maximum 8 metres and continuous straight final segment to -2 metres.
Speed sketch reflects negative velocity upward, then stays at 4 metres per second.
Acceleration sketch has horizontal levels -4 and zero and a jump at 3 seconds.
All four axes show time and suitable SI units.
Signed area or equivalent algebra gives displacement -2 metres.
Area magnitudes or split displacements give distance 18 metres.

retry.check: From $s=0$, a particle has $u=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $a=-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $5\,\mathrm{s}$, then moves at constant velocity until $t=7\,\mathrm{s}$. Sketch all four motion graphs and find displacement and distance.
retry.answer: Velocity is $5-2t$ until $t=5$, then $-5$ until $t=7$; reversal at $t=2.5$. Displacement is $5t-t^2$, with maximum $6.25\,\mathrm{m}$ at $t=2.5$, returning to zero at $t=5$, followed by $-5(t-5)$ to $-10\,\mathrm{m}$. Speed is the magnitude of velocity: V from 5 to zero to 5, then horizontal. Acceleration steps from $-2$ to zero at $t=5$. Displacement $=6.25-6.25-10=-10\,\mathrm{m}$; distance $=6.25+6.25+10=22.5\,\mathrm{m}$. Label all axes with SI units and time in seconds.

rubric.point: Velocity sketch includes reversal at 2.5 seconds and constant -5 final stage.
Displacement sketch is concave down with maximum 6.25 and a continuous straight final stage.
Speed sketch is nonnegative with a V and constant final stage.
Acceleration sketch is horizontal at -2 then zero.
Axes and SI units are labelled.
Final displacement is -10 metres.
Total distance is 22.5 metres.

forms.name: Use signed acceleration-time area as change in velocity
wordings: Find final velocity from an acceleration–time graph
Explain why area alone is insufficient for final velocity
forms.example:
A particle starts at $u=-7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Acceleration is $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $2\,\mathrm{s}$ and then $-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $3\,\mathrm{s}$. Find the final velocity.
1. First rectangle: $\Delta v_1=3(2)=6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; velocity becomes $-7+6=-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
2. Second rectangle is below the axis: $\Delta v_2=-2(3)=-6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
3. Total change is zero, so final velocity is still $-7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, not zero. The initial velocity supplies the missing starting level.
forms.check: A particle initially moves at $-5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Its acceleration is $4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $3\,\mathrm{s}$, then $-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $2\,\mathrm{s}$. Find its velocity at the end of each stage. During which stage does it reverse direction? Explain using the velocity at the stage boundaries.
forms.answer: After the first stage $v=-5+4(3)=7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; after the second $v=7-1(2)=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. It reverses during the first stage because its velocity changes continuously from negative to positive; it stays positive throughout the second stage.
forms.source: Library: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c2.1.pdf, pp.14–17; bundle M1-3.1. Pearson WPH11/01 January 2025 examiner report, PDF p.4, item 5 (Physics, not an M1 paper): https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International-Advanced-Level/Physics/2018/Exam-materials/wph11-01-pef-20250306.pdf

rubric.point: Finds first-stage velocity $+7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ using the signed change.
Finds final velocity $+5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Identifies the first stage as the reversal and explains that velocity changes from negative to positive; the second stage remains positive.
Gives velocity units.

retry.check: A particle starts at $7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Its acceleration is $-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $4\,\mathrm{s}$ and then $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $1\,\mathrm{s}$. Find its final velocity and determine whether it reverses direction during the second stage. Explain using the velocities at both ends of that stage.
retry.answer: At the start of the second stage $v=7-3(4)=-5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; at its end $v=-5+2(1)=-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. It does not reverse during that stage: velocity remains negative throughout as it increases uniformly from $-5$ to $-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

rubric.point: Finds velocity $-5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at the start of the second stage.
Finds final velocity $-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Explains no reversal in the second stage because velocity remains negative between its endpoints.
Gives velocity units.

misconceptions.idea: A negative acceleration always means the particle is slowing down.
misconceptions.temptation: In everyday speech, deceleration and negative acceleration sound the same.
misconceptions.fix: The sign only shows direction. If velocity is also negative, the speed increases; slowing down needs $a$ and $v$ with opposite signs.

misconceptions.idea: All the area between a velocity–time graph and the axis adds to displacement.
misconceptions.temptation: Areas feel like positive quantities, and the graph shows a shape, not signs.
misconceptions.fix: Area below the axis is negative displacement. Subtract it for displacement; add its magnitude only for distance.

misconceptions.idea: An acceleration–time area is always the final velocity.
misconceptions.temptation: Multiplying acceleration by time has velocity units.
misconceptions.fix: It gives the change; add the velocity at the interval start, including its sign.

misconceptions.idea: Always discard one of two positive time roots.
misconceptions.temptation: A numerical question appears to require one answer.
misconceptions.fix: Check both against the interval: a particle can pass the same height twice. Only reject a root for a physical or stated-domain reason.

misconceptions.idea: One average acceleration works in every suvat equation across several stages.
misconceptions.temptation: A single formula feels shorter than treating each interval.
misconceptions.fix: Apply suvat separately in each constant-acceleration interval, carrying velocity and position continuously across the boundary.

diagram_descriptions: Velocity against time: a straight line falls from $8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at zero seconds to $-6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at seven seconds. It crosses zero at four seconds. Shaded signed areas are $+16\,\mathrm{m}$ above and $-9\,\mathrm{m}$ below: displacement is seven metres and distance twenty-five metres. Supports graph reversal and signed-area reasoning.

Acceleration against time: a horizontal line at $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ lasts five seconds. The shaded rectangle has area $15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, a change in velocity; add the initial velocity to obtain final velocity. Supports the acceleration-time area form.

SaveMyExams XMA01 c2.2 PDF page 3: a general straight velocity–time line rises from $u$ to $v$ over time $t$. The gradient triangle gives $(v-u)/t=a$. A trapezium gives $s=(u+v)t/2$; rectangle plus triangle gives $s=ut+at^2/2$, and rectangle minus triangle gives $s=vt-at^2/2$. Supports selection of constant-acceleration equations; this is a general derivation, with no numerical check answer.
